I spent 12 months learning PySpark ETL the hard way - so you don’t have to.
These are the 33 Spark commands I wish I knew on Day 1.
(🔖Save this. You’ll thank yourself later.)
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦:
You know SQL and Pandas.
But production data = terabytes.
SQL can't scale.
Pandas runs out of memory.
PySpark? Built for this.
𝐓𝐨𝐩 𝟓 𝐏𝐲𝐒𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐤 𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫:
1️⃣ 𝐖𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐨𝐰 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬
Running totals without self-joins.
One line. Distributed automatically.
2️⃣ 𝐁𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐝𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐉𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐬
Small table + large table?
broadcast(df) = 10x faster joins.
3️⃣ 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚
.partitionBy('date') for storage.
Query only what you need.
4️⃣ 𝐂𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠
df.cache() reused DataFrames.
No re-computation. Massive speedup.
5️⃣ 𝐔𝐃𝐅𝐬 (𝐔𝐬𝐞𝐫-𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬)
Custom logic? Write once. Apply everywhere.
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐫𝐮𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐭𝐡:
Pandas: Single machine. Gigabytes max.
PySpark: Distributed. Petabytes scale.
Junior move: .apply() on Pandas
Senior move: .transform() on PySpark
𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭'𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐞𝐭:
📌 Data Extraction (CSV, JSON, Parquet, JDBC)
📌 Transformations (groupBy, join, window functions)
📌 Missing values & data cleaning
📌 Performance tuning (cache, broadcast, repartition)
📌 Advanced SQL in PySpark
📌 Stream processing (Kafka integration)
📌 ML pipelines with MLlib
📌 Cloud integration (S3, Azure, GCP)
📌 Security & compliance patterns
33 patterns total.
From beginner to production-ready.
𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐏𝐲𝐒𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐤 > 𝐏𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐬:
✅ Handles terabytes (Pandas crashes at GB)
✅ Distributed automatically (no code changes)
✅ Lazy evaluation (optimizes before running)
✅ SQL + Python (best of both worlds)
Most Data Engineers hit this wall:
Pandas works locally.
Fails in production.
PySpark solves this.
Which PySpark pattern do you struggle with most?
